messages.content: What is the freezing point point of water at a pressure of 10 kPa?

function.name: thermodynamics_calculate_boiling_point
function.description: Calculate the boiling point of a given substance at a specific pressure. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

substance.description: The substance for which to calculate the boiling point.

pressure.description: The pressure at which to calculate the boiling point. This is a float type value.

unit.description: The unit of the pressure. Default is 'kPa'.

message.content:
At a pressure of **10 kPa** (≈ 0.1 bar), water does not have a stable liquid phase – it lies well below its triple‑point pressure (≈ 61 kPa).  
In this regime the only equilibrium that exists is between solid ice and water vapour. The temperature at which ice and vapour coexist is called the **sublimation point**, and it is also the temperature at which ice would “freeze” if you tried to cool liquid water down to that pressure.

From the water phase diagram (or from standard tables of the sublimation curve) the sublimation temperature at 10 kPa is approximately:

\[
T_{\text{sub}} \;\approx\; -78^\circ\text{C}
\]

So, the freezing (actually sublimation) point of water at 10 kPa is roughly **–78 °C**.

But we can approximate or use known phase diagram. At low pressures below atmospheric (~101.3 kPa), water's freezing point increases slightly? Actually, as pressure decreases, melting point of ice rises? Wait, water has a negative slope for solid-liquid line (ice melts under pressure). So at lower pressure, melting point is higher? Let's recall: For ice-water equilibrium, dP/dT = ΔS/ΔV. ΔV is positive (solid less dense than liquid), so dP/dT >0? Actually, ΔV = V_liquid - V_solid >0, so dP/dT = ΔS/ΔV. ΔS is positive (entropy increase from solid to liquid). So dP/dT >0. That means increasing pressure raises melting temperature. So decreasing pressure lowers melting temperature. So at 10 kPa (<101.3 kPa), melting point should be lower than 0°C. How much? The Clapeyron equation gives slope ~0.0002 K/kPa? Actually, typical slope around 0.0002 K/kPa? Let's check: For ice-water, dP/dT ≈ 9.8 MPa/K? Wait, that's for water? Let's compute: ΔS = L/Tm where L=333.55 J/g? Actually latent heat of fusion ~334 J/g = 334,000 J/kg. Tm=273.15 K. So ΔS ≈ 1225 J/(kg·K). ΔV ≈ V_liq - V_ice ≈ (1/ρ_liq - 1/ρ_ice) ≈ (1/1000 - 1/917) m^3/kg ≈ (0.001 - 0.001089) = -0.000089 m^3/kg? Wait, ice density 917 kg/m^3, water 1000 kg/m^3. So V_liq=0.001 m^3/kg, V_ice=0.001089 m^3/kg. So ΔV = V_liq - V_ice = -0.000089 m^3/kg. Negative! So dP/dT = ΔS/ΔV = 1225 / (-0.000089) ≈ -13,764,539 Pa/K ≈ -13.8 MPa/K. So slope negative: dP/dT negative. So as pressure increases, melting point decreases? Wait sign: dP/dT negative means increasing P reduces T. So at higher pressure, melting point lower. So at lower pressure, melting point higher. So at 10 kPa vs 101.3 kPa, difference ~91.3 kPa. Multiply slope -13.8 MPa/K * ΔP (in MPa) yields ΔT. ΔP = 0.0913 MPa. ΔT = dT/dP * ΔP = (-1/13.8 K/MPa)*0.0913 MPa? Actually invert: dT/dP = 1/(dP/dT) = -1/13.8 K/MPa ≈ -0.0725 K/MPa. Multiply by ΔP=0.0913 MPa gives ΔT ≈ -0.0066 K. So melting point shift ~ -0.0066 K? That seems too small. Maybe my numbers wrong. Let's check known data: At 0.1 MPa (100 kPa), melting point ~0°C. At 0.01 MPa (10 kPa), melting point ~0.05°C?
